meta.title: RCC — Cronologia
meta.subtitle: Chronology of the Catholic Charismatic Renewal — global origins and the Brazilian movement (1967–present)
meta.description: An open, source-referenced chronology of the Catholic Charismatic Renewal (Renovação Carismática Católica): the 1967 Duquesne origin, the papal receptions, the arrival and boom in Brazil (Rahm, Dougherty, Canção Nova, Shalom), the Brazilian bishops' 1994 guidelines, and the ICCRS→CHARIS institutional arc.
meta.dataQualityNote: Work-in-progress dataset compiled from public sources. Movement sources (RCC Brasil, Canção Nova, CHARIS, ICCRS) are labeled as such in the references; membership numbers are the movement's own and are attributed, never asserted; the 1969-vs-1972 Brazil-arrival divergence is recorded, not resolved; sociological characterizations ('pentecostalization', competition with CEBs) are attributed to their authors. Corrections against primary sources are welcome.

threads.note: These lanes are an editorial reading of this chronology, not a neutral index. They group events by the KIND of act — the movement's origins, acts of the hierarchy, the Brazilian chapter, communities and works, discipline and review, and outside measurement — and deliberately NOT along confessional lines: no lane divides Catholic from Protestant/Pentecostal, because that boundary is contested in the sources and lanes drawn on it would make it look settled. The two pre-1960s events sit in a lane whose own label carries the attribution, because reading them as forerunners is a claim this dataset records rather than adopts. Events belong to several lanes where they belong to several storylines. Each lane states what grounds it; what was considered and left out, and why, is recorded on issue #26.

lanes.label: Antecedents (attributed, not adopted)
lanes.basis: The two events that precede the ~60-year gap in this chronology. Movement accounts read Elena Guerra as a forerunner of the Renewal, and the dataset records the Topeka/Azusa Street revivals as 'context for, not part of' the Catholic movement. This lane holds them so they are visible rather than absent, and its LABEL carries the attribution so the lane cannot be read as the dataset asserting a genealogy. A lane called simply 'precursors' would assert exactly that.

lanes.label: Origins of the Renewal
lanes.basis: The movement's own periodization: it dates itself from the February 1967 Duquesne weekend and celebrated a Golden Jubilee on that basis with Francis in 2017. This lane follows that self-dating — one of the two bases issue #26 asked to be chosen between — and so covers the 1967 foundations and the early theological consolidation, not the hierarchy's later acts, which have their own lane.

lanes.label: Acts of the hierarchy
lanes.basis: Acts by which the hierarchy positioned itself toward the movement: papal addresses, dicastery recognitions of statutes and communities, a canonisation, a penalty — and the Brazilian bishops' own Document 53. Deliberately NOT called 'Rome', because the CNBB is an episcopal conference and not the Holy See, and collapsing the two would misdescribe the document that most shaped the movement's standing in Brazil.

lanes.label: The Brazilian chapter
lanes.basis: This repo's declared second subject — its subtitle names 'global origins AND the Brazilian movement'. Stated plainly: this is a CHAPTER lane, not an act-kind lane like the others, so it deliberately cross-cuts them; the alternative was to let the repo's own second subject have no lane at all. It is not a geographic index — the place data and the map serve that.

lanes.label: Communities and works
lanes.basis: Foundations and institutional works — the covenant communities and their federation, the Brazilian communities, and the media works that grew out of them. Grouped as foundations, without ranking them or implying that the international and Brazilian bodies stand in a parent-child relation the sources do not assert.

lanes.label: Discipline and review
lanes.basis: Episcopal review of a community and a canonical penalty against a prelate associated with the movement. Kept as its own lane on issue #26's reasoning: folding these into 'communities and works' would soften them, and having no lane for them would hide them. Small by design — two events.

lanes.label: Measurement and analysis
lanes.basis: Attributed observations ABOUT the movement rather than acts OF it: survey instruments and social-scientific analysis, plus the movement's own self-reported participant figure. The lane keeps the two vocabularies adjacent but distinct, exactly as the numbers chart does — a self-report and a population share are not the same measurement and the dataset never merges them.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A movement of 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' spirituality inside the Catholic Church — prayer groups, charisms, expressive worship — born among US university students in 1967 and today present worldwide, with Brazil among its largest national expressions.

facts.label: Founding moment
facts.value: The 'Duquesne Weekend', 17–19 February 1967: a retreat of Duquesne University students at The Ark and the Dove (Gibsonia, Pennsylvania) with reported experiences of baptism in the Spirit.

facts.label: Arrival in Brazil
facts.value: 1969 per the movement's own account (Fr. Haroldo Rahm's prayer courses in Campinas), with national diffusion from 1972 via Fr. Eduardo Dougherty — an academic source (Prandi) writes 'mid-1970s', while another (Souza 2008, citing Prandi and Carranza) writes 'between 1969 and 1970'; the divergence is recorded.

facts.label: Papal reception
facts.value: Paul VI addressed the movement's Rome congress in 1975 ('a chance for the Church and for the world'); John Paul II received its leaders repeatedly from 1981; Francis created the single service CHARIS in 2019; Leo XIV addressed the Renewal on 30 May 2026.

facts.label: Brazilian scale
facts.value: The movement itself claimed ~3.8 million Brazilian participants in 1994 and tens of thousands of prayer groups today (self-reported, attributed); Pew's 2006 survey found more than half of Brazilian Catholics adopting charismatic practices.

facts.label: International service
facts.value: ICCRO/ICCRS (statutes approved 1993) served as the Rome office until 2019, when CHARIS — instituted by the Dicastery for Laity, Family and Life at Francis's express wish — replaced it; the Vatican frames CHARIS as a new service, not a fusion.

events.title: Elena Guerra's letters to Leo XIII
events.text: Elena Guerra (1835–1914), founder of the Oblate Sisters of the Holy Spirit, writes thirteen letters to Leo XIII between 1895 and 1903 urging a renewed devotion to the Holy Spirit; the encyclopedia record links the appeal to Leo XIII's 1897 encyclical 'Divinum illud munus', which established the novena to the Holy Spirit between Ascension and Pentecost. Movement bodies — Pentecost Today USA, the US national service committee, publishes the letters in English as a Renewal resource — present her as a forerunner of the Renewal; that lineage is the movement's own reading, recorded as such and not asserted here. A further movement claim, that Leo XIII consecrated the twentieth century to the Holy Spirit by intoning 'Veni Creator' on 1 January 1901, is deliberately NOT recorded: it is carried by movement accounts only and no primary act was located.

events.title: Protestant precursor: modern Pentecostalism
events.text: The Topeka outpouring (1901) and the Azusa Street revival (1906) launch modern Pentecostalism — context for, not part of, the Catholic movement.

events.title: The Duquesne Weekend
events.text: About 25 students of Duquesne University's Chi Rho group, on retreat at The Ark and the Dove, report experiences of baptism in the Holy Spirit — the founding moment of the Catholic Charismatic Renewal. Some popular accounts say 17–18 February; 17–19 is the solid dating.

events.title: The movement reaches Notre Dame
events.text: Two weeks after Duquesne, nine people — among them Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan — pray for baptism in the Spirit at the University of Notre Dame; the first 'international' gathering follows there on 7–9 April, seed of the annual Notre Dame conferences that would draw tens of thousands in the 1970s.

events.title: The Word of God community founded
events.text: Ralph Martin, Stephen Clark, Jim Cavnar and Gerry Rauch found the Word of God — matrix of the 'covenant communities'.

events.title: Arrival in Brazil (movement's account)
events.text: US Jesuit Fr. Haroldo Rahm begins 'Prayer Courses and Studies on the Holy Spirit' in Campinas in the second half of 1969 — RCC Brasil cites a 15–17 August 1969 experience with about 60 young people — and Brazil's first prayer group is born. The academic literature diverges: Prandi dates the movement's Brazilian take-off to the mid-1970s, while Souza (2008), citing Prandi (1997) and Carranza (2000), writes that the RCC 'arrived in Brazil between 1969 and 1970' with Rahm and Dougherty at Campinas; all datings are recorded.

events.title: National diffusion begins
events.text: Rahm publishes 'Sereis Batizados no Espírito', presenting 'Catholic Pentecostalism'; Fr. Eduardo Dougherty SJ, ordained 1971, returns to Brazil and spreads retreats and prayer groups across the country (movement's account).

events.title: First National Congress of the RCC
events.text: About 50 leaders meet, organized by Dougherty, Rahm and Sr. Juliette Schuckenbrock; a second congress follows in Belo Horizonte in 1974 (movement's account). The CNLB's affiliate profile likewise places the first congress in mid-1973 in Campinas and the second in January 1974.

events.title: The first Malines Document
events.text: Cardinal Léon-Joseph Suenens convenes theologians (drafting by Kilian McDonnell) and publishes 'Malines Document 1' — the theological-pastoral orientations that gave the movement doctrinal respectability.

events.title: Paul VI: 'a chance for the Church'
events.text: At the movement's third international congress in the Holy Year — with a Pentecost Mass in St Peter's on 18 May — Paul VI, addressing the participants in French on 19 May, asks: «Comment alors ce "renouveau spirituel" ne pourrait-il pas être une "chance" pour l'Église et pour le monde?» ('How then could this "spiritual renewal" not be a "chance" for the Church and for the world?'). The address was delivered in French; on vatican.va the Italian and English pages carry no body text, and the French page holds the authoritative original.

events.title: Canção Nova founded
events.text: Fr. (later Msgr.) Jonas Abib founds the Canção Nova community — the future media powerhouse of the Brazilian Renewal.

events.title: Associação do Senhor Jesus
events.text: Fr. Eduardo Dougherty founds the Associação do Senhor Jesus: publications, music and the TV program 'Anunciamos o Senhor'. The same year Raniero Cantalamessa OFMCap, a preacher close to the Renewal, is appointed Preacher of the Papal Household by John Paul II — 1980 is confirmed by the Holy See Press Office biography ('nominato da Giovanni Paolo II Predicatore della Casa Pontificia nel 1980'), an independent corroboration of what had been a CHARIS-only dating.

events.title: John Paul II receives the leaders' conference
events.text: The pope addresses the fourth international leaders' conference of the Renewal — the first of his repeated receptions.

events.title: Comunidade Católica Shalom founded
events.text: Moysés Louro de Azevedo Filho opens the 'evangelizing snack bar' in Fortaleza, with Cardinal Lorscheider present — birth of the Shalom community.

events.title: Sword of the Spirit federation
events.text: A federation of covenant communities grows out of the Word of God (unified association 1982, international entity 1983; 82 communities, 45 Catholic, by 2017). In 1990 the Word of God disaffiliated from the Sword of the Spirit — per Wikipedia and contemporary press, following an order by Bishop Albert Ottenweller after a review of the community's governance. Contemporary press (Christianity Today, 16 Sept 1991; National Catholic Reporter, 18 April 1997) described 'heavy shepherding'/'discipleship' practices; in 1991 co-founder Ralph Martin acknowledged the Sword of the Spirit disciplines had been 'an ill-advised venture' that was 'especially harmful to women' and 'fostered elitism'. A faction led by Stephen Clark then formed a separate community keeping Sword of the Spirit affiliation. These are documented criticisms and a founder's own retrospective, labeled as such — not the site's characterization.

events.title: TV Século 21 and Obra de Maria
events.text: Dougherty's association launches the satellite channel TV Século 21 (today Rede Século 21); in Recife, Gilberto Gomes Barbosa founds the Obra de Maria community, focused on pilgrimages and missions.

events.title: Pontifical recognition of ICCRS
events.text: The Pontifical Council for the Laity approves the statutes of the movement's international office, renamed ICCRS (International Catholic Charismatic Renewal Services).

events.title: CNBB Document 53
events.text: The Brazilian bishops' conference unanimously approves 'Orientações Pastorais sobre a Renovação Carismática Católica' (the Permanent Council's 34th ordinary meeting, Brasília, 22–25 November 1994, discussed, modified and approved it unanimously; the text is dated 27 November 1994, the First Sunday of Advent, and signed by the Secretary-General, Dom Antônio Celso Queiroz — so 27 November is the date of the document, not of the vote. The study began at the 32nd General Assembly in April 1994 and was completed after consultation with every diocese and dialogue with the RCC's own national commission): it recognizes the movement's fruits while imposing cautions on Bible reading, liturgy, healing practices and the relation to the local Church — the episcopate's principal 'brakes' document. No later CNBB document has superseded it; on its 20th-and-50th-anniversary reflections commentators note Doc 53 remained in force. The full text is published by Edições CNBB (the bishops' own house, digital edition); free full-text reproductions circulate via Catholic sites and a PDF mirror. Read in the full-text PDF mirror this session. Article 21 also provides that the RCC's national coordination shall have a bishop designated by the CNBB as its Spiritual Assistant, to accompany it and assist in matters of national scope 'without prejudice to the authority' of the diocesan bishop — and the document calls that body the Coordenação Nacional (the presentation says Comissão Nacional), not the Conselho Nacional the movement uses today.

events.title: The Brazilian boom
events.text: RCC Brasil itself estimated ~3.8 million participants in 1994 — a self-reported figure, attributed to the movement.

events.title: Mother of God Community placed under review
events.text: The Mother of God Community (Gaithersburg, Maryland; traced to a 1966 prayer awakening among laywomen at Our Lady of Mercy, Potomac) is reviewed at the instruction of Cardinal James A. Hickey, Archbishop of Washington, who in 1994 ordered both a self-assessment and an outside assessment. Per the encyclopedia record the external reviewer, Sr. Elizabeth McDonough, reported that members and former members described overreaching control by community leaders, including arranged marriages and scrutiny of members' finances. On 23 September 1995 Hickey addressed the community, calling it 'a gift from the Lord' while stating that lay people within it 'had too much personal authority over other people's lives', asking for leadership changes and for personal information on members to be destroyed. These are the archdiocese's and the reviewer's findings as reported, attributed — not this site's characterization. A wave-10 mining report gave the address as 25 September and named a 'Baltimore' bishop 'Nathan Hickey'; the source consulted here gives 23 September, Washington, and James A. Hickey.

events.title: Padre Marcelo Rossi's record album
events.text: 'Músicas para Louvar ao Senhor', recorded at Masses of the young priest Marcelo Rossi and released by PolyGram, sells over 3.3 million copies — the best-selling album in Brazilian phonographic history — inaugurating the era of stadium Masses and charismatic mass media.

events.title: Emmanuel Milingo excommunicated
events.text: Emmanuel Milingo, Archbishop of Lusaka from 1969 to 1983 and internationally known for a healing and exorcism ministry, was transferred to Rome in 1983 — per the encyclopedia record over what were described as inappropriate use of his office of exorcism and a role in causing divisions. He married Maria Sung in 2001 in a ceremony presided over by Sun Myung Moon of the Unification Church, drawing a public canonical admonition from Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger in July 2001. On 24 September 2006 he consecrated four married men as bishops without papal mandate; the Holy See Press Office announced the resulting latae sententiae excommunication on 26 September 2006, and he was dismissed from the clerical state on 17 December 2009. Recorded because his charismatic healing ministry made him a widely cited figure in and around the Renewal; the canonical judgments are the Holy See's, reported as such.

events.title: Pew: a 'pentecostalized' Brazil
events.text: The Pew Forum's 'Spirit and Power' survey finds 'renewalists' comprising roughly half of Brazil's population, and more than half of Brazilian Catholics adopting charismatic elements (divine healing, tongues, expressive worship) — the analysts' framing of a 'pentecostalization' of Brazilian Catholicism is theirs, not the movement's.

events.title: Canção Nova recognized by the Holy See
events.text: The Pontifical Council for the Laity recognizes Canção Nova as an international private association of the faithful (decree ad experimentum; definitive recognition later — the dates are distinct).

events.title: Shalom's definitive pontifical recognition
events.text: The Shalom community receives definitive pontifical recognition.

events.title: The RCC and Brazilian politics (analysts' account)
events.text: Social scientists (Carranza and others) describe the RCC's 'Ministério Fé e Política' backing charismatic candidates — e.g. federal deputy Diego Garcia (elected 2014, 2018) — as a response to Pentecostal political growth; the studies also record heterogeneous and internally contested engagement. The framing is the researchers', attributed. The movement's own governing text sets limits the analysts' framing does not describe: Instrução Normativa n.º 04/2021 of the RCC Brasil National Council (20 January 2021, revoking IN 03/2019) regulates the ministry during general elections and requires that MFP coordinators at every level hold no elective mandate, no commissioned or parliamentary advisory post, and no place on a party executive — while warning coordinators against 'o risco de instrumentalização de sua função' for party-political ends. Both accounts are recorded as their authors state them; neither is adjudicated here.

events.title: Pew: 'charismatic' Catholics across Latin America
events.text: Pew Research Center publishes 'Religion in Latin America' (fieldwork October 2013 – February 2014), reporting that a median of 40% of Catholics across Latin America describe themselves as 'charismatic'. Reported exposure to charismatic practice at Mass varies sharply: majorities in the Dominican Republic (77%), Honduras (61%) and Paraguay (60%) said they had witnessed such practices, while majorities in Uruguay (63%), Argentina (61%) and Puerto Rico (60%) said they never occur in their services. The 'charismatic' label is the survey's and is self-reported; these are a survey's figures, not the movement's, and are not comparable with movement membership counts. A wave-10 mining report attributed to this study a 58% figure for Brazil and about 20% for Argentina; neither was confirmed on the report page fetched for this entry, so neither is recorded.

events.title: Golden Jubilee with Francis
events.text: An ecumenical Pentecost vigil with Pope Francis at the Circus Maximus gathers ~50,000 charismatics and Pentecostals from over 125 countries, with preaching by Cantalamessa and pastor Giovanni Traettino.

events.title: CHARIS replaces ICCRS
events.text: The Dicastery for Laity, Family and Life institutes CHARIS (Catholic Charismatic Renewal International Service) at Francis's express wish; its statutes take effect at Pentecost 2019, when ICCRS and the Catholic Fraternity cease activities. The Vatican insists it is a new service, not a fusion. Francis receives the leaders on 8 June 2019.

events.title: Death of Msgr. Jonas Abib
events.text: Canção Nova's founder dies at 85.

events.title: Death of Fr. Haroldo Rahm
events.text: The pioneer of the Brazilian Renewal — and founder of the Fazenda do Senhor Jesus addiction-recovery work — dies in Campinas.

events.title: Canonisation of Elena Guerra
events.text: Elena Guerra, beatified on 26 April 1959 by John XXIII, is canonised by Francis on 20 October 2024. Movement accounts read the canonisation as recognition of a forerunner of the Renewal; the canonisation is a documented act, the lineage reading is the movement's.

events.title: Leo XIV addresses the Renewal
events.text: Leo XIV — who accompanied the Renewal during his Peruvian episcopate — receives the RCC/CHARIS, speaking on baptism in the Spirit, praise, communion and mission; he had presided at the Pentecost Mass of the Jubilee of Movements on 8 June 2025.

figures.name: Ralph Keifer and William Storey
figures.role: Lay professors at Duquesne; among the first Catholics 'baptized in the Spirit' (January–February 1967); Storey carried the movement to Notre Dame.

figures.name: Patti Gallagher Mansfield
figures.role: Student at the Duquesne Weekend and its memorialist ('As by a New Pentecost'); a living reference of the movement.

figures.name: Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan
figures.role: Notre Dame couple; authors of 'Catholic Pentecostals' (1969); organizers of the national conferences.

figures.name: Léon-Joseph Suenens
figures.role: Cardinal-archbishop of Malines-Brussels; the movement's episcopal patron; convener of the Malines Documents (1974–).

figures.name: Raniero Cantalamessa OFMCap
figures.role: Preacher of the Papal Household 1980–2024, appointed by John Paul II — the year is confirmed by the Holy See Press Office biography, independent of the movement's own sources (created cardinal 2020); the theological voice closest to the Renewal.

figures.name: Haroldo Rahm SJ
figures.role: Texan Jesuit; initiator of the Brazilian Renewal (Campinas, 1969, per the movement's account); founder of the Fazenda do Senhor Jesus recovery farms; died 2024.

figures.name: Eduardo Dougherty SJ
figures.role: New Orleans-born Jesuit; co-diffuser of the Renewal in Brazil from 1972; founder of the Associação do Senhor Jesus (1980) and Rede Século 21 (1990).

figures.name: Jonas Abib
figures.role: Salesian-formed priest, later monsignor; founder of Canção Nova (1978); died 12 December 2022 at 85.

figures.name: Marcelo Rossi
figures.role: São Paulo priest; holder of Brazil's all-time record album (1998); face of the mass-media charismatic wave.

figures.name: Moysés Azevedo and Gilberto Barbosa
figures.role: Lay Brazilian founders of the new communities Shalom (Fortaleza, 1982) and Obra de Maria (Recife, 1990).

figures.name: Michelle Moran, Pino Scafuro and Jean-Luc Moens
figures.role: Moran: ICCRS president to 2017; Moran and Scafuro were charged by Francis in 2016 with designing the single service; Moens: first CHARIS moderator (2019); Scafuro: moderator ad interim since 7 May 2021.

figures.name: Elena Guerra
figures.role: Italian religious of Lucca (1835–1914), founder of the Oblate Sisters of the Holy Spirit; wrote thirteen letters to Leo XIII between 1895 and 1903 urging renewed devotion to the Holy Spirit. Beatified 26 April 1959 by John XXIII; canonised 20 October 2024 by Francis. Movement bodies present her as a forerunner of the Renewal — their reading, recorded as such.

figures.name: Francis MacNutt
figures.role: Dominican priest (1925–2020), prominent in the Renewal's healing-prayer ministry from the late 1960s. Left the Dominican Order to marry in February 1980; received a dispensation in 1993, when the marriage was celebrated in church. Died 12 January 2020, aged 94. A wave-10 report placed his baptism in the Spirit at a 1967 Tennessee retreat; that detail is unconfirmed and is not recorded.

figures.name: Michael Scanlan TOR
figures.role: Franciscan (1931–2017); president of the College of Steubenville — later Franciscan University of Steubenville — from 1974 for 26 years, then chancellor, and a leading figure of the US charismatic covenant-community movement with roles in the Word of God and the Sword of the Spirit. Per the encyclopedia record he led the Servants of Christ the King community until he was asked to step down in 1991 amid concerns about control over members' personal lives — attributed criticism, not this site's characterization. Died 7 January 2017, aged 85.

organizations.name: RCC Brasil
organizations.relation: The national structure: National Council, state and diocesan coordinations, ministries; affiliated to the national laity council (CNLB). RCC Brasil's official history now lists the National Council presidents: Francisco Baptista (1989–1993), Erni Wienthauper (1993–1999), Reinaldo Beserra (2000–2004), Marcos Volcan (2005–2012), Katia Zavaris (2013–2019) and Vinícius Simões (2020–2025). A formal juridical constitution date for the Council is still not stated by the official source; the documented national presidency begins in 1989. Its annual Encontro Nacional de Formadores (ENF) is billed as the movement's largest formation gathering — a recurring event, not a datable founding milestone.

organizations.name: Canção Nova
organizations.relation: Community plus the Fundação João Paulo II and the Canção Nova communication system (TV, radio, web); pontifical recognition 2008.

organizations.name: Comunidade Católica Shalom
organizations.relation: New community with international presence; definitive pontifical recognition 2012.

organizations.name: Associação do Senhor Jesus / Rede Século 21
organizations.relation: Dougherty's media association and its TV network.

organizations.name: ICCRO → ICCRS → CHARIS
organizations.relation: The international office (Brussels, then Rome), recognized 1993 as ICCRS, replaced in 2019 by CHARIS under the Dicastery for Laity, Family and Life.

organizations.name: Covenant communities (international)
organizations.relation: Word of God (1967), People of Praise (South Bend, 1971), Sword of the Spirit (1982/83), Catholic Fraternity (ceased 2019 into CHARIS); the 1990s authoritarianism controversies around the Word of God are documented criticism, labeled as such. Critics and former members have likewise described People of Praise's covenant governance and defined gender roles (a member's 'head'; the 'woman leader' role, until 2017 called 'handmaid') as authoritarian — attributed criticism that drew wide media scrutiny in 2020 around Judge Amy Coney Barrett's reported association; the community states that members retain freedom of conscience under such direction. Both perspectives are recorded, attributed, not adjudicated here. The Mother of God Community (Gaithersburg, Maryland) belongs to the same thread: Cardinal James A. Hickey ordered an assessment in 1994 and addressed the community on 23 September 1995 about lay leaders holding 'too much personal authority over other people's lives'. Michael Scanlan TOR led the Servants of Christ the King until, per the encyclopedia record, he was asked to step down in 1991 over comparable concerns. Documented findings and attributed criticism, not adjudicated here.

disambiguation.note: The Renewal sits at several contested boundaries; these cards keep them straight.

items.title: RCC ≠ Protestant Pentecostalism
items.text: The movement shares practices (glossolalia, healing, praise worship) but is Catholic — sacramental, Marian, in communion with Rome, with explicit papal receptions from Paul VI (1975) to Leo XIV (2026). The 'pentecostalization of Catholicism' reading is a sociologists' framing (Prandi, Pew), not a self-description. Sympathetic narrators draw the line differently, and that divergence is itself data: CBN's 50th-anniversary feature (The 700 Club, a Protestant Pentecostal-charismatic broadcaster) tells one continuous Spirit-driven story running from Elena Guerra's letters to Leo XIII through the 1901 Kansas outpouring and the Azusa Street revival to Duquesne 1967 — presenting the Pentecostal origins as part of the same family history rather than as context.

items.title: RCC vs Liberation Theology / CEBs
items.text: The reading that the Renewal 'competed' with the base communities and represented a 'conservative renewal' (the title of Prandi's study) belongs to academic commentators; the movement describes itself as complementary to the local Church. The liberation-theology side of that story lives in the sibling tl project.

items.title: Charismatic ≠ automatically conservative in politics
items.text: There is a 'Ministério Fé e Política' and there are RCC-linked candidates, but the case studies show heterogeneous and internally contested engagement — always attributed to the analysts.

items.title: The movement ≠ the new communities
items.text: RCC Brasil (the ecclesial movement) and the 'new communities' (Canção Nova, Shalom, Obra de Maria) spring from the same charismatic current but hold distinct canonical statutes.

items.title: CHARIS: new service, not fusion
items.text: Press accounts spoke of a 'fusion' of ICCRS and the Catholic Fraternity; the Vatican and CHARIS insist CHARIS is a new service that ended both predecessors (9 June 2019). This site uses the Vatican's formulation.

branchTimeline.heading: Diffusion of the Renewal — a branching timeline
branchTimeline.note: How the 1967 Duquesne experience spread: to the US campuses within weeks, to Brazil at the end of the decade, and — from the Brazilian trunk — into the new communities that now define the movement's public face. Fork years mark first foundation; the Brazil arrival date is itself contested and is flagged on the figure.

trunk.label: Duquesne Weekend
trunk.note: About 25 Duquesne University students report baptism in the Holy Spirit at The Ark and the Dove (Gibsonia, PA) on 17–19 February 1967 — the founding moment of the Catholic Charismatic Renewal.

branches.label: US campuses — Notre Dame / Ann Arbor
branches.note: Within weeks the movement reaches Notre Dame (March 1967, the Ranaghans) and, at Ann Arbor, the Word of God community is founded — the matrix of the covenant communities and of the annual Notre Dame conferences.

branches.label: Brazil — 1969 (movement) vs 1972 (diffusion)
branches.note: Arrival is contested and recorded, not resolved: RCC Brasil dates Fr. Haroldo Rahm's first Campinas prayer group to the second half of 1969, and national diffusion via Fr. Eduardo Dougherty to 1972; the academic literature (Prandi) places the Brazilian take-off in the mid-1970s. The fork is drawn at the movement's 1969 date; the divergence is labeled on the figure.

branches.label: Canção Nova
branches.note: Fr. (later Msgr.) Jonas Abib founds the Canção Nova community at Cachoeira Paulista — the future media powerhouse of the Brazilian Renewal.

branches.label: Associação do Senhor Jesus
branches.note: Fr. Eduardo Dougherty founds the Associação do Senhor Jesus (Valinhos): publications, music and television.

branches.label: Comunidade Católica Shalom
branches.note: Moysés Louro de Azevedo Filho opens the 'evangelizing snack bar' in Fortaleza — birth of the Shalom community (definitive pontifical recognition 2012).

branches.label: Obra de Maria
branches.note: Gilberto Gomes Barbosa founds the Obra de Maria community in Recife, focused on pilgrimages and missions.

lineage.heading: Institutional arc
lineage.note: Two parallel institutional lines. The international service passed from ICCRO to ICCRS (statutes 1993) to CHARIS (2019) — the Vatican's own formulation is that CHARIS is a new service, not a fusion, shown here as a dashed step rather than a continuation. The covenant-communities line runs from the Word of God (Ann Arbor, 1967) into the Sword of the Spirit federation, from which the Word of God withdrew in 1990.

edgeLegend.indirect: A distinct step — a new service or a withdrawal, not a fusion/continuation

trees.title: International service (the Rome office)
trees.summary: From the movement's coordinating office to the Holy See's single international service.

root.name: ICCRO
root.detail: International Catholic Charismatic Renewal Office — Brussels, then Rome

children.name: ICCRS
children.detail: statutes approved by the Pontifical Council for the Laity, 14 September 1993

children.name: CHARIS
children.detail: instituted 2019 by the Dicastery for Laity, Family and Life
children.status: ICCRS and the Catholic Fraternity ceased activities at Pentecost 2019; the Vatican frames CHARIS as a new service, not a fusion of the two.

trees.title: Covenant communities (international)
trees.summary: The Word of God matrix, the Sword of the Spirit federation, and the 1990 withdrawal.

root.name: Word of God
root.detail: Ann Arbor, 1967 — matrix of the covenant communities

children.name: Word of God withdraws
children.status: The Word of God disaffiliated from the Sword of the Spirit in 1990; a faction led by Stephen Clark kept the affiliation. Contemporary press (Christianity Today 1991, National Catholic Reporter 1997) described 'heavy shepherding' practices; co-founder Ralph Martin (1991) called the disciplines 'an ill-advised venture' — documented criticism, labeled as such.

numbersChart.heading: How big is the Renewal? — contested numbers
numbersChart.note: Two different questions, two different methods. The movement counts its own participants; Pew surveys the whole population. Both bear on 'how big is the Brazilian Renewal', but they are not the same measurement — so each series keeps its own axis, its own unit and its own source label, and they are never stacked on one scale.
numbersChart.unitNote: These series use different units (absolute participants vs. share of a population) and different methods (movement self-report vs. external survey). They are shown on separate axes and are not directly comparable — only their sources make either number meaningful.
